messages.subject: interpreting allelic effects from fitqtl binary model
messages.subject_clean: interpreting allelic effects from fitqtl binary model
messages.body_plain:
I was hoping for some advice on how to interpret the allelic effect sizes ($ests) in the fitqtl ANOVA table from a stepwise model on a binary trait. I often get linked QTL, and so PVE as a measure of effect size is less satisfactory.

Given that it is a logistic regression, I assume that there is a logic link function and that the effect sizes need to be back-transformed to get the allelic effects in % (survival in my case). I also assume that some small constant is added to the 0 and 1 values because you can't take the log of 0.

Could you please give the appropriate formulate for back transforming the effect sizes from a binary model?

I have a RIL population so I am interested in getting genotypic effect sizes (2a) if it matters.

Thanks,

Chris

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] interpreting allelic effects from fitqtl binary model
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] interpreting allelic effects from fitqtl binary model
messages.body_plain:
The estimates are derived by fitting a generalized linear model with a logit link function. No constant is added to deal with the 0's and 1's; the model is fit by maximum likelihood via iteratively reweighted least squares.

If you want genotypic effects, just multiply the estimated coefficients by 2.

I don't think you can't really back-transform the regression coefficients. We have a model like:

 ln[p / (1-p)] = b0 + b1 x1 + b2 x2 + b3 x3

We can write

 p / (1-p) = exp(b0) exp(b1 x1) exp(b2 x2) exp(b3 x3)

but there's no simple way to back-transform the coefficients to a linear scale, at least to my understanding.

karl

messages.body_plain:

When I performed a QTL analysis using only Chromosome 9 markers, a new QTL (QTL A) appeared next to my QTL of interest. Nonetheless, when I performed a QTL analysis on the same phenotypic data using the whole-genome markers (markers from all chromosomes), the new QTL (QTL A) disappeared. This new QTL comes from the other parent compared to my QTL of interest. This might explain the opposite phenotypic data I am observing from my critical recombinant lines phenotypic data. But, it's just my assumption.

My question is which result should I trust: the output from markers only on chromosome 9 or the whole-genome markers analysis?

Hope to hear from you soon.

Many thanks,
Yoong

> 1. If the % variation explained by my model as a whole is 90.62517%, how come the individual QTLs from the drop one analysis add up to more than 100?
>

The %var won't add due to dependence among genotypes at the multiple QTL. Also, the %var attached to a given QTL includes the contributions from all interactions in which it is involved.

And I wouldn't trust the %var for individual QTL when there are multiple linked ones. These are calculated by looking at the residual variance with and without that term, but the effect of one QTL will get "absorbed" by linked QTL. If QTL are linked in coupling, the %var for the individual QTL will be too small; if they are linked in repulsion, it will be too big.

> The LOD scores (and %var) seemed to be increasing as I progressed with my models. Is this to be expected?

The overall LOD score and %var will increase with the addition of each term.

> 2. Can you please explain what the % variation means where there is an interaction for example individually 1...@72.0 %var = 31.366 and 2...@12.0 %var = 62.101 and where they interact 1...@72.0:2...@12.0         %var=7.311. What could this actually mean in terms of the genes involved?

I'm not sure that I can. It's basically an R^2 value. I usually think of %var explained by a QTL as the proportion of phenotypic variance that is due to variation at that locus, but that doesn't really work with the interaction.

> 3. Estimated effects. How does this cope with a DH population where all plants are either AA or BB? I had assumed that these values meant one parent providing a positive number and one providing a negative?
> I had 2 QTL quite close together on "chromosome 5" and these seemed to get closer together after I ran the refineqtl function 5...@124.0   -3.276e+00  and 5...@135.5    3.845e+00. Do you think there could just be one QTL bearing in mind each parent seems to be providing an opposite effect - how can I tell if they're additive given that the interaction has a value of 0.962? is it possible to now get output like an effect plot to visualise these interactions?

The estimated effects are like half the difference between the two genotypes, (BB - AA)/2, but estimated in the context of a multiple-regression model.

I have a hard time thinking about these effects in the presence of interactions; I prefer to look at the phenotype averages for each two-locus genotype. You can use effectplot() with a pair of loci.

  effectplot(mycross, mname1="5@124", mname2="5...@135.5")

I'd also use plotPXG to see whether the two tightly linked QTL are well supported are are due to just a few individuals.
And I'd want at least two markers between the two QTL.

> 4. How low do you go when suggesting that 2 genes are interacting? a LOD of >2 seems okay to be but what about 0.5? I feel that I lack the gut feeling that comes with experience of using this software and i'm worried about reading too much in to interactions that at the end of the day may not be very important.

I prefer to derive permutation-based thresholds from scantwo, though it is computationally intensive.

karl

messages.subject: Re: memory problem in scanone permutations
messages.body_plain:
>      we used muliple-qtl interval mapping following the procedure of caseII in your book" A guide to qtl mapping with R" ,  our population has about 10,000 snp markers and 900 RIL lines, and we used the following code:
>
> > mydata1<-calc.genoprob(mydata,step=1, err=0.01)
> > out <- scanone(mydata1, method="hk")
> > set.seed(523938)
> > out1<-scanone(mydata1, method="hk",n.perm=10000)
> Doing permutation in batch mode ...
> Error: cannot allocate vector of size 123.6 Mb
> > summary(out, perms=out1, alpha=0.05, pvalues=TRUE)
> Error in match(x, table, nomatch = 0L) : object 'out1' not found
>
> Questions:
> 1)It seems the sample size is two large,how to make the permutation work?
> 2)how to set the seed?

You can try using a smaller batch size

  out1 <- scanone(mydata1, method="hk", n.perm=10000, batchsize=50)

The permutations are being run with "batchsize" replicates at a time, and so it's producing a scanone object with that many columns, and then finding the maximum LOD score for each column. With a smaller batchsize, the object will be smaller.

But it's saying it can't make an object of size 123.6 Mb, which is not very big. So you might look at the objects in your R workspace, and remove things that are big. Perhaps do the scanone permutations in a fresh workspace that just contains the mydata1 object and nothing else.

For example, you probably don't need to keep both mydata (the original data object) and mydata1 (the object with the genotype probabilities inserted).

  mydata <- calc.genoprob(mydata, step=1, err=0.01)

In my R/broman package, I have a utility objectsizes() that will show the size of all of the objects in your workspace. (It just calls object.size() for each object in your workspace and then compiles the result.)

  install.packages("broman")
  library(broman)
  objectsizes()

You might also consider using doing the calculations just at the markers, by using step=0 (the default) in calc.genoprob:

  mydata <- calc.genoprob(mydata, err=0.01)

Or if you use stepwidth="max", it will insert only so many pseudomarkers so that no two adjacent markers or pseudomarkers are more than 1 cM apart. This will give fewer pseudomarkers and so a smaller object:

  mydata <- calc.genoprob(mydata, step=1, err=0.01, stepwidth="max")

karl

> + file="radmap8.csv", estimate.map=FALSE)
> --Read the following data:

> Warning message:
> In summary.cross(cross) :
> Some chromosomes > 1000 cM in length; there may be a problem with the genetic map.
> (Perhaps it is in base pairs?)

R/qtl needs cM locations for markers; sometimes users have included base pair locations, which causes problems. If there are positions >1000, a warning message is issued.

If the data set has no marker positions, arbitrary distances are assigned. With many markers, this will result in locations that are >1000, and so you'd also get this warning.

This is a "warning" and not an "error", so you can ignore it and go on with map construction.

karl

Karl,

I'm having problems on a cluster running Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6.3 (RHEL6.3), using Torque for resource management, and MOAB for job management. Getting permutations from scantwo is what seems to be bottoming out. I typically break up the job across 8 nodes with 4 cores per node (and use n.cluster=31), which always seems to get me 10K permutations in about 15 minutes. Most of my analyses now are running, but they seem to take 4 hours or more. I'm wondering if there is a problem with parallel being able to split the job across both multiple nodes and multiple cores per node. I've been in communication with our system admin, but he says that everything looks fine and it is difficult to troubleshoot.

On my own machine (OS 10.7), running R 2.15.1 with qtl version 1.25-15, everything works fine. I run the permutations on 6 cores and it takes about an hour. The trouble is that I have a lot of phenotypes to run and I rather not subject my computer to the sustained high temps.

Thanks,

Chris
